configurePresets.name: base
configurePresets.description: Common settings. Hidden: never configure this directly. binaryDir uses ${presetName}, so every preset gets its own build tree under build/ and switching presets never re-configures on top of another generator's cache.

configurePresets.name: dev
configurePresets.description: The everyday local preset on all three platforms. Ninja Multi-Config so Debug and Release share one configure; pick the config at build time with dev-debug / dev-release. On Windows this needs an x64 Native Tools for VS command prompt (or VS's Open Folder), because Ninja does not find cl.exe by itself — use the vs preset if you would rather not open one.

configurePresets.name: vs
configurePresets.description: Windows-only, for the Visual Studio IDE and for any shell that is not a Native Tools prompt. No generator string on purpose: 'Visual Studio 18 2026' rots on the next VS release, and with no generator CMake picks the newest Visual Studio it finds installed.

configurePresets.name: ci-linux
configurePresets.description: What the Linux CI job configures. Identical to dev plus ccache; scripts/install-linux-deps.sh installs both ninja-build and ccache, so this preset works locally too.

configurePresets.name: ci-macos
configurePresets.description: What the macOS CI job configures. brew install ccache ninja first. CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET (11.0) and CMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES are deliberately NOT set here - the root CMakeLists sets the deployment target as a normal cache STRING so a preset or a -D can still override it, and the architecture is left to the host.

configurePresets.name: ci-windows
configurePresets.description: What the Windows CI job configures. No compiler-cache launcher: sccache with MSVC needs /Z7, and juce::juce_recommended_config_flags injects /Zi in debug configs. Unblocking that means raising the CMake floor to 3.25 and setting CMAKE_MSVC_DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT=Embedded under CMP0141 - recorded here rather than shipping a cache that silently never hits.

configurePresets.name: strict
configurePresets.description: WFG_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=ON. The flag reaches wfg::warnings, which is linked to wfg_engine / wfg / wfg_tests / the spikes and NEVER to wfg_thirdparty - so a JUCE or Tracktion header warning under a future compiler cannot redden this. It inherits dev, NOT ci-linux, on purpose: this is the preset the Contributing section asks every contributor to run before opening a PR, and ci-linux pins CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache, which is not a Windows prerequisite - a Windows contributor got 'CreateProcess failed' on the first compile. The ccache launchers now live in strict-ci, which is what the Linux CI job runs. Same Ninja Multi-Config caveat as dev on Windows: x64 Native Tools prompt, or configure vs by hand with -DWFG_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=ON.

configurePresets.name: strict-ci
configurePresets.description: The CI variant of strict: identical settings plus the two ccache launchers. The Linux job runs this as a second build over the ccache already warmed by ci-linux-debug and ci-linux-release, which makes it nearly free. It exists so that `strict` itself stays runnable on a bare Windows or macOS box - and because strict-ci inherits strict, CI exercising this preset exercises every cache variable of that one, so neither can rot.

configurePresets.name: rtsan
configurePresets.description: The second net under PRD 4.2, and it catches what the allocation counter cannot: locks, syscalls and anything else that can block, not just calls to operator new. It needs Clang 20 or newer - -fsanitize=realtime does not exist before it - so this preset is expected to fail to configure on the Windows box and on macOS's Apple Clang, and that is not a defect. It lands anyway because a preset nobody can run is still the record of how to run it, and because the Linux CI job needs something to name. Tracktion is suppressed rather than fixed: its device callback takes a shared lock every block by design, which src/wfg/engine/rt/RtCheck.h explains and /godot/engine/rtForeignAllocations publishes. The suppression list is tools/rtsan-suppressions.txt and is passed at RUN time through RTSAN_OPTIONS, not here. WFG_RTSAN=1 is what turns on the WFG_AUDIO_THREAD attribute (src/wfg/engine/rt/RtCheck.h): the audio thread's entry points are marked nonblocking ONLY under this preset, so the wall of warnings that marking produces against JUCE and Tracktion arrives as a report from the job built to read it rather than as noise on three platforms that cannot act on it.

configurePresets.name: package
configurePresets.description: What .github/workflows/release.yml configures on Linux, and the parent of the other two package presets. WFG_BUILD_TESTS=OFF because the release workflow does not run the suite - CI already ran it on the commit being tagged - and a package build should not need lxml. It smoke-tests the installed binary instead (--version, selftest, validate on the shipped empty show). Build package-release, then `cmake --install build/package --config Release --prefix <dir>`: cmake/WfgInstall.cmake says what lands there.

configurePresets.name: package-macos
configurePresets.description: The macOS test build: arm64 AND x86_64, so one archive runs on Apple silicon and on the Intel Macs still in racks. Twice the compile of ci-macos, which is why only the release workflow pays it. The deployment target is the root CMakeLists' 13.3, not set here.

configurePresets.name: package-windows
configurePresets.description: The Windows test build. Inherits vs, not package, so no shell needs to be a Native Tools prompt; carries package's one cache variable by hand for that reason.

configurePresets.name: spikes
configurePresets.description: WFG_BUILD_SPIKES=ON. Its own build tree and its own CI job, so a rotted throwaway reddens a clearly labelled job instead of the product build. CI builds the spikes and never runs them - a spike ends in a written human pass/fail in docs/spikes/, not an exit code.

testPresets.name: ci-linux
testPresets.description: What the Linux CI job runs. Four at once because ubuntu-latest has four CPUs for a public repository, which this one is (GitHub's runner table, read 2026-10-13: a private repository's runner has two, and this would then be 2). Until 2026-10-13 every entry ran alone, and the whole suite was 23 minutes there, 45 on Windows and 65 on macOS; the unit suite is cut into shards (tests/CMakeLists.txt) so that there is something to run side by side. What cannot share a machine says so in its own properties - RESOURCE_LOCK, RUN_SERIAL - and is held back by ctest, never by a lower number here.

testPresets.name: ci-macos
testPresets.description: What the macOS CI job runs. Three at once because macos-latest is an M1 with three CPUs and 7 GB (GitHub's runner table, read 2026-10-13, the same for public and private repositories). Its Debug build is the slowest of the three runners by far, so it gains the most.

testPresets.name: vs-debug
testPresets.description: The whole suite on a Windows box, after cmake --build --preset vs-debug: ctest --preset vs-debug. Twelve at once, measured on the author's sixteen-core box (2026-10-13): the whole suite green in about six minutes, against some forty one entry at a time. The floor is the entries that take turns on the real audio interface (tests/CMakeLists.txt), a chain as long as the interfaces make it - it grew to eleven minutes over a morning of runs as the machine's audio engine slowed. Sixteen was no faster and not green: the chain is as long whatever the number, and so many at once starved the tick thread and plugins' children enough to fail the checks that are judged off CI because they time the tick. An entry is more than one busy core - a driver is a Python process, a wfg serve and sometimes a plugin's child - which is why the number is below the cores. The drivers that judge an engine keeping time take turns in lanes, one per four processors where GITHUB_ACTIONS is unset at configure time (tests/CMakeLists.txt): four here, the whole suite green in 296 s on 2026-10-13, against 700 s with all of them in one lane as on CI. On another machine, ctest -j with about three quarters of its cores.

testPresets.name: ci-windows
testPresets.description: What the Windows CI job runs. It inherits vs-debug, as the ci-windows configure preset inherits vs, so the job exercises the local preset's settings too. Four at once because windows-2025 has four CPUs for a public repository (GitHub's runner table, read 2026-10-13; two for a private one, and this would then be 2). Kept at four after the first run at four (38350416745) failed eleven drivers here: what they shared was running four at a time, seven or eight engines on four CPUs, and they now take turns on the `realtime` lock instead (tests/CMakeLists.txt). The same suite held to four of the author's efficiency cores with GITHUB_ACTIONS set was green at four, in 779 s, and again with a second stream of unit shards on those cores beside it, in 798 s. TWO SINCE 2026-10-13: on the runner itself four was not: TG.9's run (38392873762) failed a different engine-timing check on each attempt - pair-link's main found again on its port and ui.show-settings exiting past its 120 s, then phase9c-take's silence while it records - each green alone, each starved by the unit shards running beside the realtime lane. Windows was the fastest of the three test jobs at four (about 32 minutes against Linux's 54), so two costs the run nothing it waits for.
